column3: It closely repeats the focus's counterfactual: a calamity followed by the claim that a messenger and signs should have come first.
Moses is sent with signs and manifest authority, illustrating the advance provision of evidence invoked by the focus.
Noah's open warning to his people exemplifies a messenger addressing a community before its accountability.
The Moses mission joins messengerhood, a sign from the Lord, and freedom from torment, concretely instantiating the focus's requested prevention.
The immediately preceding objection demands a sign, and its answer supplies the documentary evidence that the focus develops into the no-excuse claim.
It limits destruction by denying that a reforming people are destroyed unjustly, supporting the focus's procedural account of punishment.
Their despair before rain gives only a distant temporal contrast to the focus's before-punishment condition.
The destruction of earlier prosperous generations gives broad historical background but adds no prior-warning dimension.
Messengers announce a coming destruction of an unjust town, linking messenger arrival and a punitive outcome.
Acceptance of a previously known revelation is a limited counterpart to recognizing evidence before the claimed punishment.
The next ayah's mutual waiting completes the local sequence after the focus's counterfactual excuse.
Following divine pleasure rather than returning with wrath offers only a broad outcome contrast.
The demand for an angelic sign is answered with the warning that its descent would settle the matter without delay.
It explicitly connects earlier denial of signs, their sending, and warning, closely clarifying the focus's demand-for-sign setting.
Its command concerning companionship and desire does not clarify warning, evidence, or punishment before excuse.
The announcement of painful punishment lacks the focus's prior-message or excuse dimension.
Destroyed earlier generations function as visible evidence for later hearers, supporting the focus's insistence that warning is available.
The destruction of the first Aad is a bare historical instance without the focus's messenger-and-sign rationale.
Those facing the Fire wish to return so they could stop denying signs and become believers, exposing regret after evidence is no longer actionable.
The warning that disgraceful punishment will come, followed by waiting, parallels the focus's warning-before-outcome sequence.
It joins messengerly endurance, proclamation, and destruction limited to the defiantly disobedient, though less directly than the focus.
Its prior criminal peoples and destruction provide only a general precedent for punishment.
The statement that Thamud was not spared is a minimal destruction parallel without a warning rationale.
It affirms that messengers have conveyed their Lord's messages, supporting the focus's premise that notice has been delivered.
It directly anticipates the claim that a book would have led to greater guidance, then answers it with already-arrived proof, guidance, and mercy.
Facing punishment on the Day relates to outcome but not to the focus's prior-warning procedure.
It specifies that towns were destroyed for wrongdoing and that a fixed term was set for their destruction.
The prayer for a messenger who recites signs, teaches the Book, and purifies supplies the positive content of the messenger sought in the focus.
Worldly disgrace and greater final punishment add only a broad counterpart to the focus's humiliation and punishment.
The declaration of messengerhood before Pharaoh is a redundant instance after the fuller Moses mission already appears.
The prayer not to be disgraced at resurrection invokes messengers but does not explain warning before punishment.
It states that settlements face destruction or severe punishment under what is inscribed, a close backdrop for the focus's counterfactual destruction.
The destruction of similar groups is a general precedent with no stated advance warning.
The messenger declares that he has conveyed what he was sent with before warning of replacement, supporting fulfilled notice.
Earlier deniers receive punishment unexpectedly, a useful contrast to the focus's claim that evidence had already been available.
The question about destroying earlier peoples is too compressed to add a distinct warning or evidence connection.
It records the destruction of stronger towns but not the prior delivery that grounds the focus's excuse argument.
Following earlier peoples with later ones gives only a broad pattern of successive punishment.
Moses receives the Book after former generations were destroyed, as insights, guidance, and mercy for later remembrance.
Belief in a prior scripture offers limited confirmation of earlier documentary continuity.
Noah's call links forgiveness and delay until an appointed term, showing warning as an opportunity before an irreversible end.
The sending of birds against an army does not illuminate messengerly warning or a post-punishment excuse.
It portrays a demand that revelation be made explicit while identifying it as guidance and healing for believers.
The reference to Noah's earlier transgressive people provides only generic historical judgment.
Denial of the Lord's signs leads to destruction, supplying a causal counterpart to the focus's appeal to following those signs.
Mutual waiting for punishment shares the focus's anticipatory posture but not its no-excuse logic.
Noah is sent specifically to warn his people before painful punishment reaches them, directly matching the focus's procedural sequence.
Messengers bring clear proofs to their peoples before retribution on criminals, giving a compact parallel of evidence and consequence.
The redeemed acknowledge that messengers came with truth, but the Paradise scene only indirectly supports the focus.
The promise to messengers and divine retribution do not add the focus's notice-before-punishment relation.
It directly continues the same pattern of demanding a sign after truth arrives while recalling earlier rejection of Moses' evidence.
Rejection of a messenger is followed by destruction, giving a basic but redundant consequence pattern.
A messenger's community is divided over what was sent with him and waits for divine judgment, preserving the warning-and-response setting.
Destruction of crops and offspring through corruption is not the focus's judicial punishment after offered guidance.
The request for an impending punishment supplies only the punishment side of the focus.
Moses seeking instruction and following guidance is a distant counterpart to following signs.
Its appeal to prior and present revelation has limited relevance but does not frame warning before punishment.
Denial of the two messengers results in becoming among the destroyed, a concise parallel of rejected notice and outcome.
The question about possessing an earlier book touches documentary authority but not the focus's specific excuse.
The command to follow the recitation only lightly parallels the focus's wish to follow divine signs.
A messenger says he conveys what he was sent with while his people remain ignorant, supporting the focus's premise of communicated warning.
The messenger's self-description as trustworthy is a redundant, generic instance without signs or punishment.
Joseph came earlier with clear proofs, yet persistent doubt was followed by a renewed claim that no messenger would come after him.
Being among the most abased for opposing God and His messenger only loosely echoes the focus's disgrace.
A messenger recites signs, purifies, and teaches the Book to people formerly in clear error, expanding the remedial role sought in the focus.
This repeated messenger declaration adds no marginal clarification after equivalent candidate formulations.
Division among communities and return to God do not address prior warning or signs.
Conduct toward God and His messenger does not clarify why a messenger must precede punishment.
The non-prophetic sending in this narrative is unrelated to the focus's divine messenger and signs.
Following charity with injury is unrelated to following divine signs before punishment.
The gradual withdrawal of a shadow has no focused relation to the ayah's procedural argument.
This repeated messenger declaration adds no marginal value after the same formula has recurred.
The destruction of stronger earlier generations rebukes self-reliance but omits the focus's antecedent guidance.
This repeated messenger declaration adds no marginal value after prior identical candidates.
The denial of a heavenly sign as bewitchment does not clarify the focus's warning-excuse sequence.
Hypocrites' verbal recognition of the messenger, exposed as false, only distantly concerns response to a messenger.
The people demand divine punishment after being confronted, a pointed contrast to the focus's later claim that warning was absent.
This repeated messenger declaration adds no marginal value after identical earlier candidates.
The sending of devils against disbelievers is not analogous to dispatching a messenger with signs.
The remains of destroyed generations are presented as signs for people who walk among their dwellings, supplying public evidence before denial.
A personal sign for Zachariah is unrelated to the communal proof-and-warning argument.
The mention of God's messenger in a warning about usury does not explain the focus's prior mission.
Disbelievers refuse the Quran and earlier scripture, showing rejection of available evidence but not the focus's procedural sequence.
The oath by those sent is too indeterminate to add a usable messenger-and-warning link here.
A personal sign for Zachariah is unrelated to the focus's communal proof-and-warning argument.
A messenger's recitation, purification, and teaching broadly parallels the guidance content, but repeats stronger candidates.
Disbelief in signs and murder of prophets and justice-commanders are answered with painful punishment, linking rejected guidance to consequence.
Following victorious magicians contrasts only vaguely with following divine signs.
Return to God after death does not clarify messengerly notice before punishment.
The claim that time destroys people is a counterpoint to the focus's attribution of destruction to God, but not its warning rationale.
Seeking to hasten punishment echoes the punishment demand without the focus's prior guidance condition.
The command to follow a straight path is a general guidance counterpart, distant from the focus's messenger-and-sign formulation.
The wish for a reminder from earlier peoples illustrates the kind of claimed lack of guidance answered by the focus.
Care for believing followers concerns the messenger's community but not prior evidence before punishment.
Turning away from vain speech does not add to the focus's warning-excuse argument.
The arrival of messengers at Lot's family is an incomplete narrative instance without its warning or outcome.
The sending of winds for revival is unrelated to the sending of a human messenger and signs.
Noah's warning to his people of a great day's punishment directly supplies the advance-warning side of the focus's claim.
The description of two gushing springs is unrelated to the focus's warning and excuse structure.
Sending warners among prior peoples broadly parallels the focus, but comes after stronger, more explicit warning-before-punishment examples.
Messengers bring good news and warning so that people have no argument against God after their arrival, directly stating the focus's no-excuse principle.
The Messenger comes after an interval so the People of the Book cannot say that no bearer of good news or warner came to them.
Jinn and humankind are asked whether messengers came reciting signs and warning of the meeting of the Day, directly joining signs, warning, and accountability.
Messengers came to the destroyed towns with clear proofs, but their inhabitants would not believe what they had previously denied.
Every community has a messenger, and when its messenger comes judgment is made between them with justice.
Earlier generations were destroyed after their messengers brought clear proofs and they still would not believe.
A messenger was raised in every community with the call to worship God and avoid false powers, establishing broad prior notice.
A messenger came to the people, but they denied him; punishment then seized them while they were wrongdoers.
It expressly denies punishment until a messenger has been sent, the governing principle assumed by the focus's counterfactual.
Messengers are sent as bearers of good news and warners, while disbelievers dispute against truth and mock the signs and warnings.
No town is destroyed without warners, directly supplying the warning-before-destruction rule behind the focus.
The reminder accompanying the preceding destruction rule affirms that such destruction is not unjust.
The Lord does not destroy towns until He sends a messenger to their central settlement reciting His signs.
No community has passed without a warner among it, giving the wider historical premise for the focus's claimed advance notice.
Those who vowed they would follow guidance if a warner came are shown to turn away when warning arrives.
The people entering Hell are asked whether messengers came reciting their Lord's signs and warning them of this Day's encounter.
Messengers came with clear proofs, but disbelief was followed by divine seizure, closely paralleling rejected evidence before punishment.
The keepers of Hell recall that messengers came with clear signs, reinforcing that the condemned had received notice.
Messengers came to the people from before and behind them with the call to worship God, but they rejected the message.
Whenever a warner is sent to a town, its affluent leaders invoke inherited practice, illustrating resistance to received warning.
As each group is cast into Hell, its keepers ask whether a warner had not come to it.
The condemned acknowledge that a warner did come, but they denied him and rejected the revealed warning.
